reconcile.note: Clarke identifies Job's 'morning stars' with the angelic host created alongside the 'heavens' of Genesis 1:1, not the literal stars of day four.
reconcile.halfLine: This pole reads Job's morning stars as an angelic host present at creation, not literal stars formed on Genesis' fourth day.

discrepancy.note: Keil, Delitzsch, and the Pulpit Commentary read Job's 'morning stars' as actual stars present at creation, keeping Genesis' fourth-day timeline in tension.
discrepancy.halfLine: These commentators take Job's morning stars as literal stars already shining at creation, holding Genesis' fourth-day sequence in tension.

quotes.text: They are actual stars… the fulness of light, in which the morning stars shone forth all together at the founding of the earth, may symbolize one grandly harmonious song of joy.
quotes.attr: Keil & Delitzsch (Delitzsch d. 1890), Biblical Commentary on the OT

quotes.text: The stars generally, or the actual stars visible on the morn of creation, are probably meant… Their priority to the earth is implied, since they witness its birth.

sides.snippet: God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night. He also made the stars.
sides.verseText: God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night. He also made the stars.

sides.snippet: When the morning stars sang together, And all the sons of God shouted for joy?
sides.verseText: When the morning stars sang together, And all the sons of God shouted for joy?
